title: Here's one bit of good news for Mass Effect: modders are bringing the multiplayer mode to Mass Effect Legendary Edition
author: Jody Macgregor
content:
When Mass Effect 3's beloved multiplayer mode was left out of the Legendary Edition, there was much wailing and gnashing of teeth. Redemption has finally come in the form of the ME3Tweaks modding team, who have spent the last three years quietly working to not only get multiplayer working, but improve it.

"It's not just a ME3MP port but rather an extensive remaster of the experience," says modder Audemus. "This includes new features like bringing forward LE's native features like controller support/HDR, overhauled UI, rebaked level lighting, upscaled/redrawn textures, upgraded shaders, improved networking/server replication, extensive bug fixes, new gameplay modes, and a stable format for future mod support and easy installation/compatibility."

They're even adding new game modes, like one called "Unified" that combines enemies from multiple factions, and letting players either join ME3Tweaks' server, or set up their own private servers.

The ME3Tweaks team are the same modders who previously revived and revised the Pinnacle Station expansion, a lost DLC for the original Mass Effect that was also left out of the Legendary Edition. They're planning to release the multiplayer mod on N7 Day, which is also when composer Sam Hulick plans to release a re-scored version of the leaked Mass Effect Universe trailer.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. A former music journalist who interviewed everyone from Giorgio Moroder to Trent Reznor, Jody also co-hosted Australia's first radio show about videogames, Zed Games. He's written for Rock Paper Shotgun, The Big Issue, GamesRadar, Zam, Glixel, Five Out of Ten Magazine, and Playboy.com, whose cheques with the bunny logo made for fun conversations at the bank. Jody's first article for PC Gamer was about the audio of Alien Isolation, published in 2015. Jody edited PC Gamer Indie from 2017 to 2018, and he eventually lived up to his promise to play every Warhammer videogame.

title: “I Play the Field; I Read Around.”
author: Maggie Shipstead
content:
Editor’s Note: Passages is a members-only monthly newsletter about life-changing encounters with stories. Each edition of Passages features a short essay in which one of our favorite writers explores their own life as a reader. Our first contributor, Maggie Shipstead, is an accomplished travel writer whose most recent novel, Great Circle, was shortlisted for the Booker Prize and the Women’s Prize for Fiction. Join Longreads today to receive Passages in your inbox, along with our weekly Top 5 story recommendations and other member perks.

When I was a kid, my mom called the stack of books on my nightstand a “smorgasbord.” People use a lot of food language when they talk about reading. We devour; we gulp. I like to “graze” as a reader, moving through multiple books simultaneously, dipping in and out according to my mood. Romantic metaphors, too, come in handy, alluding to the vagaries of appetite and compatibility and taste. I would say that I’m still not a monogamous reader. I play the field; I read around.

The current count of books I’m partway through is eighteen: eight print books, eight e-books, and two audiobooks. There’s some nonfiction in there: Into the Ice by Mark Synnott, Boom by Michael Shnayerson, and the audiobook of Entitled by Andrew Lownie, which, if you need to be convinced that Prince Andrew is one of the most odious people on the planet, boy do I have the book for you. The majority of my docket is taken up by novels, though. A galley of Emily St. John Mandel’s new book Exit Party is on my nightstand, as is Ian McEwan’s What We Can Know. (Bad title! I hate titles that are unmemorable strings of nonspecific words!) I’m in a race to finish Venetian Vespers by John Banville before Libby, the public library app, takes it back for maybe the fourth time. The Banville is short and enjoyable but has been a victim of the smorgasbord approach, never quite seizing priority. Also on my Libby shelf are, among others, Lovers XXX by Allie Rowbottom, The Original by Nell Stevens, and Villa Coco by Andrew Sean Greer. On my Bookshop.org app, I have The Remembered Soldier, a magnificent novel by the Dutch writer Anjet Daanje that is very long and that I ended up (happily) buying because I didn’t want to race Libby’s loan period.

I wasn’t an early adopter of e-books, partly because my first novel was published in 2012, at the height of e-book doomerism, when everyone was saying print books were soon to be a thing of the past and e-books were the enemy. (Interestingly—at least to me—the ratio of print copies to digital has gone up for each of my three successive books, with only that first one selling more e-books than physical.) The Kindle launched in 2007, but I didn’t have an e-reader until 2013, when I got a Kobo in a gift bag. I liked it, but the process of acquiring e-books and getting them on the device was cumbersome, and, anyway, within a year I left it on an airplane. 

During the pandemic, I found myself meandering back toward e-books. I’d had an iPad for a while but didn’t really know what to do with it until a friend told me about Libby. Somehow I’d forgotten libraries existed, and I didn’t have a card for the Los Angeles system, even though I’d lived in the city for six years by then. I signed up for one online, downloaded the app, and everything changed. I didn’t even have to leave my house, which I wasn’t supposed to do anyway.

I’d never lost the habit of reading in bed at night, but my intake of books had slowed dramatically over the years, probably starting in college. I was an English lit major, so reading was work. Then writing became my job in my mid-20s, and that professionalism wore away any playfulness that was left in reading. I’d gotten timid and precious in my choices, only buying books I felt confident I would enjoy but then often not enjoying them after all, at which point they would linger, stubbornly material, in my house until I rounded up a box or two to donate. With Libby, I could be capricious again. Every time I came across an intriguing mention of a book or someone recommended one, I placed a hold. I would then immediately and completely forget about the hold until, days, weeks, or months later, some vaguely recalled title appeared on my iPad, a gift from my past self. Something about the convenience and low stakes of Libby got me reading like I hadn’t in years. I became a filter-feeder, opening my maw to take in books indiscriminately, unbothered by the ones that must be spat out. In 2020 I read 60 books; last year I read 92. I started but didn’t finish dozens more.

The dream, though, even for a nonmonogamist like myself, is The One, the book that makes all others disappear, that enchants you completely and exclusively until the last page boots you back out into the world. That feeling of absorption is one I crave, and I’ve experienced it many, many times, courtesy of books of all different genres and the whole spectrum of high- to low-browness. Last week it was the audiobook of Patrick Radden Keefe’s London Falling. In January it was a re-read of Ariel Levy’s memoir The Rules Do Not Apply. Lately I’ve been immersed in Michelle Huneven’s back catalog. Possibly the most delicious experiences of The One emerge from a perfect alchemy of time, place, and book, like when I found an orange and white Penguin edition of The Secret History in a used bookshop in Bali in 2011 and, having somehow never heard of it, bought it on the basis of the title alone. Or when I read Persuasion on my phone in a tent in the Swedish Arctic. Or when, traveling alone in New Zealand, I read all the Twilight books in rapid succession, and upon finishing the last one, felt like I’d woken up in a bus stop, disheveled and hungover and utterly mystified as to how I’d gotten there. 

The One is not singular but takes infinite forms. There is no heartbreak when you move on. In fact, the pleasure is additive. A writer friend reminded me of this once when I was expressing disgruntled envy about the reception of someone else’s book. “No one ever finishes a good book and says, ‘Now I’ll never read another book again,’” she said. 

Free love prevails at the smorgasbord. And, I mean, there’s a title.

Three Reading Recommendations

  • In 2017, before a total solar eclipse made a nice long arc over the continental US, I read “Total Eclipse” by Annie Dillard for the first time. I’d had no plans to bestir myself to go see the eclipse, but I pretty much finished the last paragraph, bought a tent and some welder’s glass to look through, got in the car and drove from LA to Oregon. The eclipse—and you have to be in the path of totality—remains the most astonishing thing I’ve ever seen. Conveying the power of natural phenomena is extremely difficult, and Dillard’s writing elicits both the visceral shock of seeing a total eclipse and the necessity to witness one with your own eyes.
  • Look, call me unexciting, but I would be pretending to be someone I’m not if I didn’t include a New Yorker piece. How to choose, though? I love an unsolved/unsolvable mystery, so should I pick Douglas Preston’s piece about the Dyatlov Pass incident? Or pretty much anything by Patrick Radden Keefe? Or perhaps the 2009 profile of Caster Semenya by Ariel Levy that changed my understanding of gender and biological sex? I think because I can only pick one, I’ll go with Levy’s “Thanksgiving in Mongolia,” which you’ve either already read and been undone by or everyone you know has already told you to read and for some reason you haven’t. Her alchemy of experience into writing is somehow both raw and polished and hits with the force of a train.
  • Recently I was reminded of this piece by Alexandra Paul, “Stalked: A Baywatch star’s 13-Year Nightmare,” when I happened to interview her twin sister, Caroline. It’s a harrowing personal account of being stalked for many years, and also includes meaningful practical advice for how to protect ourselves in this age of frightening access. I’d always had deep ambivalence about not responding to a horrible poison pen DM I got on my wedding day, and Paul’s essay granted me total certainty that not engaging had been the right move all along.

Maggie Shipstead is the New York Times-bestselling author of three novels and a short story collection. Her novel Great Circle was shortlisted for the Booker Prize and the Women’s Prize. She is a graduate of the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, the recipient of a fellowship from the National Endowment for the Arts, and the winner of the Dylan Thomas Prize and the L.A. Times Book Prize for First Fiction. Her travel writing and essays have appeared lots of places. She lives in Los Angeles.

title: Ghosts of the Grove
author: Krista Stevens
content:
Palmeros harvest medjool dates by hand by leaping into the crown of a tree “full of thorns sharp enough to puncture a tire—or, say, a human limb.” For Offrange, Ashley Stimpson introduces us to the workers who carry on a proud, 6,000-year-old farming tradition that’s in danger of dying out, just as date sales take off in the United States. (Photos by Siri Kaur.)

As far as harrowing job descriptions go, the palmero is up there with trapeze artist and surgeon. Must like heights, must work well in punishing heat, must feel comfortable yielding lethally sharp hand tools. In addition to brute labor, the job also requires an aptitude for botanical minutiae: the pungency of a ripening spadix, the dusky translucency of a perfectly ready date.

Palmeros spend most of their year in the top of the palm trees, which are dioecious plants, meaning male and female reproductive organs grow on separate trees. While the wind can carry pollen from tree to tree, it results in an unpredictable and uneven yield. Around 4000 BC in the Persian Gulf, our ancestors got wise and started cultivating the date palm by hand, kicking off a tradition Medina and Patino still carry out today.

More picks by Ashley Stimpson

Ashley Stimpson | Sunday Long Read | April 9, 2023 | 5,236 words

“Creamer wasn’t just coming up against locals’ attachment to their horses, but a pernicious human tendency to confuse profound affection for animals with wisdom about what’s best for them.”

The Many Ways Scientists are Turning Birds into Feathered Field Assistants

Ashley Stimpson | Audubon Magazine | February 25, 2025 | 2,212 words

“From frigatebirds and gulls to curlews and cormorants, researchers are tapping the ”Internet of Animals” to map, understand, and protect our changing world.”

Ashley Stimpson | Popular Mechanics | September 18, 2025 | 4,110 words

“As automakers lobby to yank AM radio from new models, broadcasters argue that the trusty 105-year-old medium is an irreplaceable lifeline for millions of Americans. But is anybody listening?”

title: The November argument session begins on Monday
author: Nora Collins
content:
Skip to main content

Newsletter

Oct 30, 2026

It was a relatively quiet week at the court, as the justices – and the SCOTUSblog team – prepared for the November argument session to begin next week. On the interim docket, the court decided one immigration-related dispute and moved closer to being able to decide another.

At the Court This Week

On Thursday, an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church urged the Supreme Court to deny the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. For more on their filing, see the On Site section below.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court denied a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that prevents enforcement of a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to pause certain deportation proceedings. There were no noted dissents.

Morning Reads

Supreme Court isn't on the ballot. But in campaigns, it is hotly contested

Bart Jansen, USA Today

Congress may be “the battleground in the 2026 midterm elections,” but the Supreme Court is playing a role in many races, according to USA Today. Republican and Democratic candidates alike are highlighting “disputes about the high court’s membership, its size and its ethics” and calling on voters to keep these battles in mind when they head to the polls next week. In particular, candidates are raising the possibility of a Supreme Court vacancy during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office and emphasizing that the party that controls the Senate will be able to determine whether another Trump nominee is confirmed to the court.

‘Mountain of evidence’: ICE agents discriminated against Latinos, judge says

Brittny Mejia, Los Angeles Times

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong has “barred immigration agents in Southern California from stopping people based on racial stereotypes,” citing what she described as “a mountain of evidence” showing that agents are “targeting people who appear Latino,” according to the Los Angeles Times. “The injunction … requires agents to establish individualized reasonable suspicion before detaining someone for immigration enforcement.” The Times noted that the evidence cited by Frimpong in her new order “had not yet been turned over by the government when the Supreme Court last year stayed the judge’s earlier order barring stops based solely on race or ethnicity, language, location or employment, either alone or in combination.” Frimpong acknowledged the Supreme Court's decision in her new order, but emphasized that the court “had not explained its reasons for granting the stay.” “This Court cannot be faulted for failing to follow guidance that was never given,” the judge wrote. The Trump administration has indicated that it will appeal Frimpong’s order to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

Utah charges Kalshi and its founders, escalating a fight over who can regulate prediction markets

Marc Levy, Associated Press

On Wednesday, Utah “filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity,” according to the Associated Press. “The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.” The AP noted that “[t]he felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the U.S. Supreme Court.”

Law school puts AI 'Supreme Court' to the test

Karen Sloan, Reuters

Last week, the University of North Carolina School of Law “tested whether AI could replicate the reasoning of US Supreme Court justices” by staging “a simulated Supreme Court argument based on an actual case the high court heard in 2025,” according to Reuters. Participants found that although the three AI justices used in the test drew the same conclusions as the real-life justices, “deciding the case the same way the actual court did,” the bots did not excel at mimicking their behaviors during oral argument. “The AI justices asked questions and hypotheticals of the law students who argued the case, but their interactions felt robotic and they didn’t interrupt or interject the way the real justices do.” “There’s still this huge gap in it actually feeling human,” said Nicole Downing, the law school’s assistant dean for AI, to Reuters.

Trump Wants to Kick ‘Rogue Activist Judges’ Off Cases. Can He?

Adam Liptak, The New York Times

In his newsletter for The New York Times, Adam Liptak explored the Trump administration’s battle against what it describes as “rogue activist judges,” a category that has come to include judges who expressed frustration with government lawyers or criticized the administration’s actions in media interviews. Liptak noted that the Supreme Court held, in a 1994 opinion from Justice Antonin Scalia, that “[e]xpressions of impatience, dissatisfaction, annoyance and even anger” are “within the bounds of what imperfect men and women, even after having been confirmed as federal judges, sometimes display” and do not necessarily establish “bias or partiality.”

On Site This Week

Case Preview

Court to hear argument in religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado

By Amy Howe

The court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools. The schools argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because the state will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

From the SCOTUSblog Team

The Supreme Court and what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment

By Kelsey Dallas

(SCOTUSblog Plus) Earlier this month, the concept of cruel and unusual punishment briefly captured the country’s attention after the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30 tried and failed to execute Christa Pike. The botched execution drew attention to a range of past rulings on the death penalty, while also highlighting a number of unresolved issues in this fraught area.

Contributor Corner

Two cheers for “insecure originalism”

By Richard Re

In his Controlling Opinions column on Wednesday, Richard Re reflected on Justice Samuel Alito’s effort in his new book to discourage judicial “insecurity” – that is, “a judge’s self-conscious worry that he might be advancing his own policy preferences under the guise of impartial adjudication.” According to Re, “what Alito labels insecurity is better understood as a form of humility and self-awareness,” impulses that are laudable, not problematic.

From the SCOTUSblog Team

Another Trump term?

By Amy Howe

As it currently stands, the 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor. But that could soon change, because by mid-January the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review from the Trump administration or Trump himself.

Contributor Corner

The Trump administration’s attempt to prevent noncitizen voting and the role of the Supreme Court

By Edward Foley

In his Justice, Democracy, and Law column on Tuesday, Edward Foley explored a growing battle over the division of authority between states and the federal government when it comes to “determining who can vote in congressional elections and regulating how the voting process occurs.” One such case involves the issue of alleged noncitizen voting in California, which may soon arrive at the Supreme Court.

Contributor Corner

When the Supreme Court blessed zoning

By Anastasia Boden

In her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1926’s Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty, in which the Supreme Court, after rehearing the case and “a dramatic reversal in several justices’ positions,” paved the way for modern zoning. Boden noted that “[t]hree justices dissented, though they never said why.”

Podcasts

Advisory Opinions

Bringing Charges Against the President’s Political Enemies

Sarah Isgur and David French zoom in on the cases prosecutors have brought against political enemies of the Trump administration. Then, they review the latest news from the battle over a Washington, D.C., golf course before tackling the administration’s sue-and-settle case in Texas.

Amarica's Constitution

The Innocent Ham Sandwich

The election is upon us, and worries about possible anti-democratic actions have many on alert. Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka peer ahead to see what to watch out for and review the relevant constitutional law and history.

A Closer Look

Justice John McKinley

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice John McKinley, who served on the court from 1838 to 1852.

With the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act of 1837, Congress added two more seats to the court. The first went to Justice John Catron, and the second went to Justice John McKinley, whose confirmation created a nine-justice court. While the seat itself was an honor, its duties were less so, as McKinley would discover.

McKinley was born in May 1780 in Culpeper County, Virginia. His family soon moved to Kentucky, where he taught himself law, passed the bar in 1800, and practiced in both Frankfort and Louisville. After moving to Alabama around 1818, McKinley grew wealthy from land speculation, partnered with Andrew Jackson in the Cypress Land Company, and helped found the city of Florence, Alabama. Jackson himself called McKinley “the most prominent man” in the state.

McKinley entered the Alabama Legislature in 1820, and, after backing Jackson for the presidency (he had previously supported Henry Clay), won a U.S. Senate seat in 1826. In the Senate, McKinley advocated for bankruptcy policies “favorable to small farmers.” However, his vote to override Jackson’s Maysville Road veto (the Maysville Road Bill essentially proposed federal stock purchases for internal improvements, like state roads) raised doubts about his loyalty, and he was not reelected in 1830. After one term in the U.S. House and another in the state legislature, he won a second Senate term in 1836, only to leave the seat within two months due to his Supreme Court appointment.

In 1837, the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act expanded the court to nine justices, and Jackson’s advisers pushed McKinley for one of the new seats, but Jackson preferred his friend William Smith instead. When Smith declined, the pick then fell to the newly inaugurated President Martin Van Buren, who went with McKinley. Van Buren gave McKinley a recess appointment in April 1837, and the Senate confirmed him by voice vote that September.

After his nomination, McKinley wrote to then-House speaker James Polk that he had “accepted the appointment, although it is certainly the most onerous and laborious of any in the United States.” The new 9th Circuit included Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, and eastern Louisiana and required eight circuit terms a year. McKinley told Polk he would travel more than 5,000 miles annually, although McKinley later reported a figure closer to 10,000. The duties also likely ate into his finances (the justices were required to personally pay for their own circuit court duties) and took a toll on his health (he later had a paralyzing stroke on his way to Jackson, Mississippi).

Even before his first term started, McKinley asked Van Buren in person about changing the new 9th Circuit, but the president left the issue out of his next annual State of the Union, upsetting McKinley. Following McKinley’s first full term, the justices disbanded in March 1838 to “confront some 6,000 cases on their cumulative circuit dockets,” according to Steven Brown, who wrote McKinley’s first full-length biography. McKinley’s share from the 9th Circuit alone made up 4,700 of those.

Brown detailed one of the more interesting stories from McKinley’s extensive circuit duties in a 2011 Journal of Supreme Court History article. In April 1839 while holding circuit court in Jackson, a fight spilled into the courtroom and an officer of the court (who had been called “a stupid jackass” by McKinley for not bringing in the court marshal) pulled McKinley’s nose. Newspapers reported that the justice swore never to return to Jackson, and McKinley referenced the “gross personal indignity” in a letter to Van Buren.

In his 1839 State of the Union address, Van Buren told Congress that the circuit’s schedule and distances made it “impossible” for its judge to keep up. McKinley missed much of his circuit duties, along with the entire 1840 term, due to illness. Combined with his failure to hold court in Arkansas for almost five years, states in his circuit felt “neglected,” and the Mississippi Legislature called for McKinley’s impeachment. Congress eventually reorganized the circuits in August 1842, relieving McKinley of Mississippi and Arkansas; beginning in 1843 he rode the reconstituted 5th Circuit, which covered Alabama and Louisiana.

As for McKinley’s actual approach to cases, he was strongly for states’ rights, supporting them “over the authority of the federal government.” During his time on the court, McKinley wrote 19 majority opinions, four dissents, and two concurrences by one count, 22 opinions by another, and 23 by a third, the lowest per-term rate of his era. One of his opinions for the court was in 1845’s Pollard’s Lessee v. Hagan, where he held that new states enter the union on equal footing with the original 13, including ownership of the lands beneath navigable waters. Four years later in the 1849 Passenger Cases, McKinley argued in his concurrence that the federal government, not the states, controlled immigrants arriving from overseas until they became permanent residents of the states.

Increasingly ill after a stroke in 1842, McKinley died in Louisville in July 1852 at age 72, after 14 relatively difficult years on the court. He was replaced by Justice John Archibald Campbell, also from Alabama.

SCOTUS Quote

JUSTICE O'CONNOR: "A light bulb exploded."

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: "I think we're... I think it's safe."

JUSTICE BREYER: "A light bulb went out."

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: "It's a trick they play on new Chief Justices all the time."

(Laughter.)

JUSTICE SCALIA: "Happy Halloween."

— Central Va. Community College v. Katz (2005)

title: Defending the Midterms from Donald Trump
author: @NewYorker
content:
The reporter Barton Gellman discusses threats to the upcoming elections.

October 30, 2026

Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up for our daily newsletter to get the best of The New Yorker in your inbox.

Amid all the prognostication about which party will emerge triumphant during the midterms, there has also been increasing alarm: Will it be a free and fair election? As soon as Donald Trump returned to office, he began making moves to create disruption—demanding private voter data from states, threatening election officials with jail time, and even seizing ballots from prior elections to investigate alleged fraud. And although, so far, none of the White House’s efforts have threatened to significantly alter the results, the Department of Justice has hinted that there is more to come. The U.S. Attorney General, Todd Blanche, has not ruled out using the force of law to prevent election certifications. Furthermore, a lawsuit from the Trump Administration against the State of Alaska is already under way, before a single vote has even been counted. The reporter Barton Gellman and David Remnick discuss the threats to the midterm elections and Gellman’s new piece, “The State Officials Defending the Midterms from the President.”

Further reading:

  • “How ICE Is Targeting the 2026 Midterms,” by Jonathan Blitzer
  • “What the Gerrymandering Wars Mean for the Midterms—and 2028,” by Isaac Chotiner
  • “The G.O.P.’s Latest Voter-Suppression Plan,” by Sue Halpern

title: Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Use AI to Vote
author: @wired
content:
As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence–powered chatbot.

Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.

But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.

Even supposedly nonpartisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.

Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections, and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.

According to the Forum AI research, almost 40 percent of election answers given by all the mainstream chatbots contained at least one factual error. In August, when Forum AI’s researchers asked why someone should vote for North Carolina congressman Don Davis, Claude gave a response that conflated the lawmaker with a “former school superintendent” of the same name.

Google and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Open AI directed WIRED to a blog outlining the company’s approach to elections in 2026.

Part of the problem is that chatbots are reliant on an increasingly problematic pool of online information. Research by NewsGuard found that mainstream chatbots cite so-called “pink slime” websites nearly 50 percent of the time when asked about candidates and policies related to the midterms. Pink slime sites present as mainstream news websites but are in fact funded by political or ideological groups and individuals.

Ahead of the midterms, many more of these sites have sprung up, and chatbots are paying attention. The worst offender, according to NewsGuard, was OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which cited the pink slime sites in more than 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok chatbot performed best, citing pink slime sites in 30 percent of cases.

“I don't think that most Americans are prepared to navigate an election in the age of consumer AI,” Nina Jankowicz, executive director of the American Sunlight Project and a former disinformation czar during the Biden administration, tells WIRED. “One of the problems is that executives and companies have really overpromised on what AI is capable of. It has to ingest this information from somewhere, and often those sources are not very good. And it's predictive, so if it doesn't know the answer, it does frequently make things up.”

title: A Collapsing Star Produced an Afterglow Brighter Than Its Galaxy - Nautilus
content:
Much of what we understand about the universe comes from interpreting the light patterns that hit our telescopes—from the smallest twinkles of distant stars to giant clouds of dust and gas. That’s what makes the recent find from NASA’s Fermi Gamma Ray Space Telescope, which sits in low Earth orbit, so exciting: it’s one of the brightest bursts of light in decades.

The flash is an intense afterglow following a gamma-ray burst (GRB). While the gamma-ray light was modest, the afterglow was incredibly bright—among the brightest 1 percent of observed events compared in a newly published study.

Read more: “Dead Star Offers a Glimpse Into Our Solar System’s Future”

Why was the afterglow so much brighter than the event itself? 

The team behind the study thinks it has to do with the angle of our view. “We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” study author Roberto Ricci said in a statement. “We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.”

What happened first was the death of a massive star around 2 billion light-years away. As stars collapse, they shoot out brief, intense jets of gamma rays from their poles, which was the first flash spotted by the Fermi telescope on March 10th.

As the jets of gamma rays continue to spread out through space, they collide with the surrounding gas and start accelerating particles, which glow with energy released as radiation (i.e., the afterglow). The GRB 260310A afterglow brightened gradually over several hours, until it was outshining its galaxy. It then faded, only to brighten again weeks afterward in the X-ray spectrum. That may have been the light from the narrow core of the gamma-ray burst finally escaping, the astronomers say.

Such an intense, long-lasting afterglow suggests that what would have been dismissed as a fairly standard gamma-ray burst may in fact have been much more intense, viewed from the right angle. “What appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet’s core,” study author Yu-Han Yang said in a statement. “Our models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the sun’s energy output into a pencil-thin beam.”

With increased telescope performance and broader sky-mapping capabilities, scientists hope to capture more gamma-ray bursts from a greater range of angles in the future—which will, in turn, improve our understanding of how giant stars die off.

After all, there’s a lot that you can glean from a beam of light.

title: Court seems poised to side with Catholic preschools in religious discrimination dispute
author: Amy Howe
content:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared ready to hold that the exclusion of Catholic preschools in Colorado from the state’s universal preschool program violates the First Amendment. After just over two hours of oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a majority seemed to agree with the challengers that Colorado’s refusal to provide them with an exemption from rules that would require the preschools to admit all students – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents – should be subject to a more stringent constitutional test than that applied by the lower court. The court could decide to apply that standard itself or send the case back to the lower courts for them to do so. 

Colorado launched the universal preschool program, which provides families in the state with up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools, in 2023. To participate in the program, preschools must meet a variety of state standards and sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” The preschools cannot decline to serve LGBTQ families, because Colorado believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs – the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children – went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy. They contended that requiring Catholic preschools to agree to the nondiscrimination agreement to participate in the universal preschool program constitutes unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to carve out a religious exemption that allows them to take part in the program.

After both the district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the challengers’ claim, they came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to take up the case – which the court agreed in April 2026 to do.

Representing the challengers, Nicholas Reaves told the justices that the schools in the Archdiocese of Denver “exist to pass on the faith to the next generation.” “[T]his is not a zero-sum game,” he said, because “letting Catholic schools” participate in the universal preschool program “will create more seats for everyone.”

Representing the state, Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton countered that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools to” the program and allows them to teach their religious beliefs. It simply asks them, she emphasized, to comply with the same rules as everyone else.

One of the major points of contention at Tuesday’s argument was the significance of the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction. The case was the third in a trilogy of decisions on the availability of public funding for religious institutions. In Carson, the majority applied strict scrutiny – the toughest constitutional test – after it concluded that the Maine law barred some private schools from receiving public funds “solely because they are religious.”

In response to a question from Justice Clarence Thomas about whether a ruling for the challengers would require the court to extend its ruling in Carson, Reaves responded that it would not. In Carson, he insisted, the court’s “focus … was to look at … what is happening to the religious believer?” The court in Carson, he said, “didn’t focus on the text of the law in Maine. It focused on whether schools are being excluded on account of their religious exercise.”

Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Reaves on that point, observing that the law at issue in Carson specifically discriminated against religious schools – which, Roberts suggested, is not the case with the Colorado program.

Reaves pushed back. He noted that the laws in other cases involving public benefits had been neutral, rather than discriminating against religious people or organizations – for example, the court’s 1963 decision in Sherbert v. Verner, reversing a ruling by the South Carolina Supreme Court that had rejected a constitutional challenge to the denial of employment benefits from a Seventh-day Adventist whose religion barred her from working on Saturday.

Roberts later questioned Norton on a related point, asking her to differentiate the Colorado program from the law at issue in Carson and telling her that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here.” He also told Norton that the state was trying to “bury Sherbert” even though “nothing in our precedent has backed away from” it.

Two of the court’s Democratic appointees, however, echoed Roberts’ initial skepticism that Carson dictated the outcome of the challengers’ case. Justice Elena Kagan told Reaves that the trilogy of cases culminating in Carson involved laws that had excluded religious institutions and schools because of their religion. “[I]t was a nondiscrimination principle,” she emphasized, but “you’re asking us to” issue a decision that would go “far beyond” its earlier cases. In particular, she suggested, the challengers were seeking a ruling that religious people “need a special accommodation” because of their faith.

Reaves responded that an interpretation of the court’s decision in Carson that focused on whether the law at issue expressly discriminated against religion would be “very easy to circumvent.”

Kagan responded that this isn’t “a good case to raise the kind of specter of circumvention.” “[T]his is a case,” she continued, “of a state trying to enforce its own nondiscrimination principles.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to agree. She characterized Carson as a case that prohibited governments from treating religious schools worse than it treated secular schools. That doctrine, she posited, was “pretty narrow” and made “perfect sense.” But, she told Reaves, “your schools want to discriminate by exclusion” when no other school participating in the universal preschool program does so.

Some of the court’s Republican appointees were more persuaded by the challengers’ argument – also advanced by Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the challengers – that Carson should apply even if the Colorado law does not specifically target religion.

Justice Neil Gorsuch, for example, asked “what would be left” of cases like Sherbert “if everything turned on express discrimination” against religion, while Justice Samuel Alito appeared dubious that the legislators who enacted the Colorado universal preschool law “would not understand what the effect of” the law’s requirements “would be.”

Similarly, Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Norton why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows “schools will be unable to agree to?” Barrett pointed to a New York Times op-ed written in the wake of Carson by law professor Aaron Tang, who she stated suggested that states counteract some of the effects of Carson by enacting nondiscrimination requirements.

Norton resisted any effort to link Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement to an intent to target religious schools, stressing that there was no evidence of the legislature’s motives and (in response to a question from Jackson) that the requirement predated the inclusion of religious schools in the program.

The justices and advocates also debated, although less extensively than the significance of Carson, whether Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that are subject to a less stringent constitutional test, known as rational-basis review.

Reaves told the justices that the Colorado nondiscrimination requirement was not the kind of “across-the-board” prohibition that the court envisioned in Smith because the Colorado law contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catch-all” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation. Moreover, he added, the law also creates exceptions to accommodate children with disabilities and children from low-income families.

For her part, Norton characterized the preferences as very different from the kind of exclusion that the challengers seek. Even if a school receives a preference, she stressed, it is still subject to the nondiscrimination requirement.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh appeared to approach the case from what he regarded as a practical angle, asking Norton why the state wouldn’t “seek the win/win?” With over 2,000 preschools participating in the Colorado program, he said, there should be “plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers” and, at the same time, “the ability of LGBT parents” to find a school that is a good fit for their families. “Why,” he asked, “has this been provoked?”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor took a different tack, suggesting that a ruling for the challengers could have broader implications. A Catholic preschool, she told Reaves, could reject a child “merely” because his or her parents are LGBTQ. Would this, she queried, also allow a religious preschool to turn down Black children?

Reaves said that it would not. He pointed to a 1983 case in which the Supreme Court, applying strict scrutiny, upheld the Internal Revenue Service’s decision to revoke the tax-exempt status of a private university and private school with racially discriminatory admissions policies. The government in that case, he emphasized, indicated that its interest in prohibiting such policies was not merely “compelling” (the first factor under strict scrutiny) but “overriding.”

He told the justices that strict scrutiny should similarly apply to this case. “And then the government can come forward and say we have a really good reason for” excluding Catholic preschools from the program. But, he concluded, “we just don’t think they’ve done that in this case.”

By the end of the argument, Sotomayor seemed to leave little doubt about where she stood. “No matter what line of cases we follow,” she said, “there will be tremendous problems and a great cost to someone.”

A decision is expected sometime next year.

Recommended Citation: Amy Howe, Court seems poised to side with Catholic preschools in religious discrimination dispute , SCOTUSblog (Nov. 3, 2026, 3:45 PM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/court-seems-poised-to-side-with-catholic-preschools-in-religious-discrimination-dispute/

title: Wise Words from Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas as to Access to Court Records
content:
My Stanford law school colleagues Nora and David Engstrom, as well as Berkeley law professor Jonah Gelbach and others, have asked the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules recommend a new Rule of Civil Procedure (5.3) governing the sealing of court records. I think this is an excellent idea: While there is a good deal of precedent on the question, distilling it into a rule that can easily be consulted by judges, lawyers, law clerks, and pro se litigants would be very helpful.

Just today, Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas (also a former law professor), submitted a letter endorsing the proposed rule, and I thought it was much worth passing along:

Dear Members of the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules:

I write to express my strong support for proposed Rule 5.3, a much-needed recapitulation of the procedural standards governing sealing of judicial records.

The public has a presumptive right to access judicial records. This right serves several important societal functions. By exposing the records of private wrongdoing to the public eye, this right deters further wrongdoing. By forcing the government to litigate out in the open, it empowers the public "to keep a watchful eye on the workings of public agencies." Nixon v. Warner Commc'ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 598 (1978). And by enabling the public to dig into the bases for judicial decisions, it enables the public to assure itself of the strength of judicial reasoning, the cornerstone of judicial legitimacy. This right thus not only "diminishes possibilities for injustice, incompetence, perjury, and fraud," but also provides "the public with a more complete understanding of the judicial system and a better perception of its fairness." In re Avandia Mktg., Sales Prac. & Prod. Liab. Litig., 924 F.3d 662, 672 (3d Cir. 2019) (internal quotation marks omitted).

On paper, this right looks strong. In the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where I sit, a district court issuing an order to seal "must articulate the compelling, countervailing interests to be protected" and "make specific findings on the record concerning the effects of disclosure." Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). But that standard is a paper tiger—mighty in appearance, but toothless in practice. Time and again, we see cases on appeal where the parties asked to seal large parts of the record below, and the district court, with little discussion, agreed to do so.

Take one recent motion to seal in a Third Circuit case. The district court had certified a multi-state class action against a car company. On appeal, the company asked us to seal ten volumes of appendices, totaling nearly three thousand pages of material. The company told us that sealing was necessary to prevent competitors from copying its design choices, stealing its engineering solutions, and exploiting its sales strategy.

But it took only a cursory glance at the appendices to see how overbroad the company's request was. Hundreds of pages, for example, covered deposition testimony from one of the plaintiff's lay witnesses, a mechanic who had worked on the defendant's cars and had commented on their alleged defects. Hundreds of other pages dealt with one of the plaintiffs' experts, who had opined on the veracity of the defendant's public comments and sales catalogues. But if the mechanic based his testimony on his day-to-day work on the defendant's cars, and the expert had based his testimony on the company's public statements, how would these materials reveal competitive secrets? So I denied the request without prejudice, asking the company to come back with a narrower request if it so chose. But why had the record below been sealed in the first place?

It should come as little surprise that motions to seal almost always go unopposed. The harm of overbroad sealing falls on future victims of repeat tortfeasors, future litigants in related cases, and the public at large. It does not fall on the parties to the case.

Indeed, the parties generally have an active interest in secrecy. The party who moves to seal records fears that the information produced in the case could lead to bad press coverage, competitive harms, or even follow-on litigation. The other party presumably does not share those same concerns about broad disclosure, but it does not share the public's concerns about overbroad sealing, either.

So in the give-and-take game of litigation, where it can be important to reserve your capital for fighting the fights that matter to your client, opposing a motion to seal is a waste of that capital. At the very least, it is a waste of time and money. For lawyers in an active dispute—so used to viewing themselves as only agents of their clients, and not also officers of the court—submitting an opposition to an overbroad motion to seal might not seem worth the cost of the paper to print it.

This leaves it to district-court judges to police these motions and protect the public's presumptive right of access to judicial records. But what my experience as a judge on the court of appeals has taught me, Professor Engstrom et. al's empirical work now confirms: Most district courts rubber-stamp these requests.

This might come as a surprise to some members of the Judicial Conference. After all, the law of every circuit requires district courts to reject requests to seal that are too broad to be justified by their supposed rationale.

So why do district courts frequently fail to apply that law? One problem might be the lack of developed precedent in this area. Because motions to seal are almost never subject to full treatment in district court opinions, let alone appellate review, there are few decisions applying legal standards to specific facts, teasing out what interests suffice to justify sealing, and how broad is too broad. Without clearly factually analogous precedent to rely on, district courts might be more hesitant to deny a motion to seal as overbroad, even though the operative legal standard compels that result.

Another problem is rooted in the lack of adversarial presentation. With no one on the other side, inflated claims of confidentiality go unchallenged.

Other problems might boil down to the mechanics of busy district court dockets. Perhaps, for example, when a district court grants a protective order, that decision generates an inertial force that skews the outcome of the subsequent motion to seal, even though the two decisions are subject to different legal standards. Or perhaps a motion to seal, because it is unopposed, slips under the radar, resembling an administrative matter to be rubber-stamped rather than a legal decision to be carefully scrutinized.

But whatever the reason, the results are clear: For most motions to seal, "the parties agree, the busy district court accommodates, and nobody is left in the courtroom to question whether the decision satisfied the substantive requirements." Binh Hoa Le v. Exeter Fin. Corp., 990 F.3d 410, 417 (5th Cir. 2021).

This proposed rule will push parties and courts alike to do better. First, this proposed rule will ensure that the parties know what their obligations are when they submit a motion to seal. I often sit by designation on the District of Delaware, where I regularly receive motions to seal with no accompanying explanation or justification, putting the onus on me to push the parties for more. Under Proposed Rule 5.3(c), parties will be reminded that, as our circuit has regularly held, "[b]road allegations of harm, bereft of specific examples or articulated reasoning, are insufficient." In re Avandia Mktg., 924 F.3d at 673 (internal quotation marks omitted).

Second, this proposed rule will act as a process-forcing mechanism for busy district court judges. District courts lack the benefit of adversarial litigation over motions to seal. And without a party opposing a motion, it is easy to think that no reasoning is needed for an order—if no party loses, the thinking goes, no party needs a basis for the court's decision.

Proposed Rule 5.3(h) makes clear that even without an adversarial party, the district court must act as the steward of the public interest in accessing court records, and must reason through its decision. The decision to seal is for the court to make by applying the correct legal standard, not for the parties to make by means of consent. Proposed Rule 5.3(i) provides a checklist that a district court can use in reaching that decision.

Finally, the proposed rule will remind parties and district courts alike that sealing is not an all-or-nothing question. Proposed Rule 5.3(d)(3) and (g) make clear that, where viable, the default approach should be targeted redactions. The choice is not between disclosing a list of social security numbers and sealing an entire document. A happy medium is often readily available.

This proposed rule does not make new law. Sunlight is the best disinfectant for many societal ills, yet sealing "insulates the participants" in the legal process, "masking impropriety, obscuring incompetence, and concealing corruption." Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. v. F.T.C., 710 F.2d 1165, 1179 (6th Cir. 1983). Judicial reasoning is the basis for judicial legitimacy, yet sealing "withdraws an element of the judicial process from public view," making "the ensuing decision look more like fiat." Matter of Krynicki, 983 F.2d 74, 75 (7th Cir. 1992) (Easterbrook, J.). For these reasons, the courts of appeals have consistently held that the public has a presumptive right to access judicial records, one that should only be abrogated where necessary, and even there only to the extent necessary. This proposed rule simply makes that right harder to neglect.

My then-student Jennifer Welson and I had unsuccessfully proposed a sealing rule to the Rule Committee in 2020, on behalf of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and Electronic Frontier Foundation; but I much hope that the Engstrom et al. proposal, which is backed by considerably more empirical research than mine had been, will be more successful.

title: "Would 'Go Luigi'" Was a Threat, and Thus Subject to Harassment Prevention Order Statute
content:
From D.M. v. A.M., decided by Massachusetts Appellate Court Justices Ariane Vuono, William Meade & Zachary Hillman on Oct. 21:

The defendant, A.M., appeals from the extension of a harassment prevention order …..

To review a civil harassment prevention order, "we consider whether the judge could find, by a preponderance of the evidence, together with all permissible inferences, that the defendant committed acts that constituted one of the enumerated forms of harassment." As relevant here, "[h]arassment" is defined as "[three] or more acts of willful and malicious conduct aimed at a specific person committed with the intent to cause fear, intimidation, [or] abuse." To qualify, the conduct must be intended to cause and actually cause fear of physical harm or damage to property….

Here, as the District Court judge properly found, there were three or more incidents constituting harassment. On June 27, 2025, the defendant called the Target store that D.M. managed, looking for D.M., and became vulgar with the employees when she was told that D.M. was not there.

On June 28, 2025, the defendant showed up at the Target store and demanded to speak to D.M. The defendant then called Target's customer service line and made multiple threats, including that she would "go Luigi" and that she was "at the point of feeling like Luigi" and that D.M. was "gonna be sorry though."

On June 30, 2025, the defendant called Target again, looking for D.M., and stated, "this is why people go full Luigi." {The judge noted, and we agree, that the defendant was referencing Luigi Mangione, who at the time was accused of murdering Brian Thompson, the Chief Executive Officer of UnitedHealthcare.}

On July 1, 2025, the defendant called again and stated that she would continue calling and coming to the store looking for D.M. The judge properly found that these events constituted three or more incidents of harassment ….

The defendant's repeated calls and trips to the Target store and her references to Luigi Mangione reasonably support an inference that she intended to cause D.M. fear, intimidation, or abuse. Additionally, as the judge properly found, D.M. was "petrified" from these threats, moving to work at a different location to avoid the defendant. Therefore, the judge did not err in extending the harassment prevention order….
